items.content:
Your instructor

Elena Park

Former foundation program officer, nonprofit consultant, and the person who taught you that program officers read your budget before your narrative.

About Elena

Eight years reading proposals. Now teaching what actually works.

Elena Park spent eight years as a program officer at a regional community foundation in the Pacific Northwest. In that time, she reviewed more than four hundred grant applications — from single-page letters of inquiry to 40-page federal proposals — across program areas including workforce development, housing, early childhood education, and arts and culture.

What she saw, year after year, was that the organizations with the strongest programs often wrote the weakest proposals. Not because they lacked skill or intelligence — but because nobody had ever taught them how foundation staff actually read applications. They'd learned grant writing through trial and error, through old templates from former colleagues, or through brief workshops that covered the vocabulary but not the judgment.

"The proposals that stayed with me weren't the most polished ones. They were the ones where I could feel the program officer had actually thought about what I needed to know — where the budget told the same story as the narrative, and where the outcomes were honest about what was actually measurable. That's a teachable skill. That's what this course is."

In 2018, Elena left the foundation to start her own consulting practice, working with small and mid-sized nonprofits across the country on proposal development and funder strategy. Her clients range from neighborhood mutual aid organizations writing their first foundation grant to established social service agencies retooling a stagnant development program. She's helped organizations raise their first six-figure grant, build a diversified funder portfolio from scratch, and — perhaps most meaningfully — stop spending months on applications that were never going to score.

Why a course, why now

Elena designed Practical Grant Writing after noticing a pattern in her consulting work: many development coordinators, program managers, and executive directors were writing grants as a secondary responsibility — squeezed into a workweek already at capacity, without institutional knowledge or dedicated support. The skills they needed weren't exotic. They were learnable. But there wasn't a focused, practitioner-led course that treated them like the capable professionals they were.

The course is structured around the decisions Elena saw trip up even experienced proposal writers: whether to apply, how to frame need, what an evaluation plan needs to include, and what a budget that looks credible actually looks like. Each week is grounded in real examples and designed to apply immediately to work students are already doing.

Who this course is for

Practical Grant Writing is designed for development coordinators, program managers, and executive directors at nonprofits without a dedicated grant team. You don't need prior grant writing experience — but the course will be most useful if you're already in a role where grant writing is part of your responsibilities, or is about to become one. If you've been writing grants by instinct and want to understand the reasoning behind what works, this course is for you.

Six-week course

Curriculum

Week by week, you'll build every major skill required to write competitive grant proposals — from your first funder research call to your final submission checklist.

01
Week One — September 10

Reading Funders Like a Program Officer

Most proposals fail not because the writing is bad, but because the funder was a bad fit. This week, you'll learn to decode RFPs, read foundation websites like an insider, and make fast, confident go/no-go decisions. Elena draws on her years reading proposals to walk through what funders are actually looking for — and the signals most applicants miss.

  • Decoding RFPs
  • Foundation websites
  • Go/no-go decisions
  • Alignment signals
  • Strategic prioritization
02
Week Two — September 17

The Need Statement — Making the Case

Your need statement is where most proposals lose or win a reviewer's confidence. This week covers how to research and frame community need with precision — using data effectively without overwhelming the narrative. You'll learn the "deficit frame" trap and how to write about need in a way that centers your community's strengths while making a compelling case for your program.

  • Community data research
  • Deficit framing
  • Asset-based language
  • Evidence sourcing
  • Narrative structure
03
Week Three — September 24

Project Design & Theory of Change

Reviewers need to believe your program will work — and that you understand why it will work. This week you'll build a logic model or theory of change for your own project and learn how to describe your program's activities, outputs, and connections to funder priorities in clear, confident language. We'll workshop examples in class together.

  • Logic models
  • Theory of change
  • Activities vs. outputs
  • Implementation timelines
  • Funder alignment language
04
Week Four — October 1

Outcomes, Metrics & Evaluation Plans

Weak outcomes are one of the most common reasons good programs get passed over. This week you'll write SMART outcomes and craft a proportionate, credible evaluation plan — without a research staff or a $20,000 external evaluator. Elena explains what program officers actually look for in an evaluation section and what level of rigor is realistic for different grant sizes.

  • SMART outcomes
  • Output vs. outcome
  • Data collection methods
  • Realistic evaluation plans
  • Reporting expectations
05
Week Five — October 8

Budgets That Tell the Story

The budget is the second document a program officer reads — and it should reinforce your narrative, not contradict it. This week covers line-item budget construction, budget narratives that explain your numbers in plain language, indirect costs, matching funds, and the specific errors that raise red flags for foundation staff reviewing your application. We'll look at real budget examples, including ones that didn't make it.

  • Line-item budgets
  • Budget narratives
  • Indirect costs
  • Matching funds
  • Common red flags
06
Week Six — October 15

From First Draft to Submission & Beyond

In the final session, you'll bring together everything from the course into a submission-ready process. We cover revision strategies, proposal-specific proofreading, submission logistics, and — crucially — how to build a grant calendar and reusable materials library so your next proposal takes half the time. You'll leave with a working template kit that belongs to you.

  • Revision process
  • Submission checklists
  • Grant calendars
  • Reusable boilerplate
  • Long-term systems

6 live sessions with Elena

90-minute Tuesday sessions with instruction, examples, Q&A, and group discussion. Recordings available within 24 hours.

Weekly worksheets

Practical exercises designed for a real grant you're currently working on. Apply the skills immediately to your actual proposals.

All session recordings

Every session recorded and accessible to you permanently. Rewatch any section as many times as you need, on your schedule.

Reusable template kit

A grant calendar template, organization boilerplate bank, and reusable narrative sections — yours to keep and customize after the course.

Lifetime course access

Return to any session recording or worksheet whenever you need it. No expiration — the course stays useful as long as you're writing grants.

Cohort community

Learn alongside other development professionals. Share challenges, exchange feedback, and build connections with peers who do this work too.
